topics.title: Problem I Probably Didn't Make!
topics.text:
This is a problem that I made that is similar to a problem in the UTD Team Contest at AMSP 2017. I am not sure whether someone has thought of it before, but here it is.



A knight (the chess piece) starts in one of the four squares in the middle of an 8 x 8 chessboard. What is the minimum number of steps it has to make so that it reaches every square? (Ex. It starts in one of the four squares, then takes x moves to go to the top corner, then goes in a snake like pattern until it reaches the end and it takes 2 moves to go to the next square. The value of this would be x + 63(2) = x + 126. You do the same thing but with starting in the other three squares and you get x + 136, x + 146, and x + 156, your final answer would be x + 126. The order of which the knight reaches each of these squares does not matter. The square the knight starts in does not count as starting in that square.



Attached is an example of where the knight can start from.

topics.title: Generalization
topics.text:
I decided to find the sum $1(1+1)+2(2+1)+3(3+1)+4(4+1)\cdots(n-1)n+n(n+1)$, and found out that each term was $2\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}=2\cdot T_n$, and factored a $2$ out to get $2(T_1+T_2+T_3+T_4\cdots +T_{n-1}+T_n)$. Using the "sum of triangular numbers" formula, I then had $2\cdot\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6}=\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3}$.



So, with my formula, I tested out a sample case: $n=1$. This gave me $2$. Success!



Then, I used mathematical induction to get $\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3}+(n+1)(n+2)=\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3}+\frac{3(n+1)(n+2)}{3}=\frac{(n+3)(n+1)(n+2)}{3}$, which is right.



But, being me, I wanted to generalize it. (I have a bad habit of generalizing things when I see them.) So is there a generalization for $1(1+n)+2(2+n)+3(3+n)+4(4+n)\cdots +(m-1)(m-1+n)+m(m+n)$, or am I just seeing things and being crazy?

topics.title: Favorite applications of theorems/identities/forumulas
topics.text:
Math is a great thing and I really enjoy it, so I decided to make this thread to see people's favorite ways of applying theorems, identities, formulas, and whatever else to problems so people can see how nice the ways of solving certain problems can be. Just post what you think is a really neat way of an application of a formula. I'll start with a problem my friend made (maybe it exists somewhere else already but it was the first time I saw it).



P1: FactorizingFind the number of factors of $2^{20} - 2^{18} - 3$.


S1$2^{20} - 2^{18} - 3 = (4)(2^{18}) - 2^{18} - 3 = (4-1)(2^{18}) - 3
(3)(2^{18}) - 3 = (3)(2^{18} - 1)$.

Now we factor using difference of squares.

$2^{18} - 1 = (2^9 + 1)(2^9 - 1)$

Now we factor both of these factors using sum/difference of cubes.

$2^9 + 1 = (2^3 + 1)(2^6 - 2^3 + 1) = (9)(57)$

$2^9 - 1 = (2^3 - 1)(2^6 + 2^3 + 1) = (7)(73)$

Then we add back the $3$ from before.



So $2^{20} - 2^{18} - 3 = (3)(9)(57)(7)(73) = 3^4 \times 7^1 \times 19^1 \times 73^1.$ The number of factors is $(4 + 1)(1 + 1)(1 + 1)(1 + 1) = 40$.



I thought that this was a very nice application of using the sums/differences of squares and cubes factorizations. I highly enjoyed solving the problem like this and it was a good algebra exercise as well as something to enjoy.




Please feel free to share your own favorite solutions!

topics.text:
I decided today to make up an interesting problem. We have a point in a rectangular pool, and a stick. What is the shortest length of the stick so that for any place where you put the dot, the stick can touch it.



Note that the stick can't go over the edge of the pool, one end of it must be touching the edge.  That's cheating, because then if it's two inches from the edge and the stick is, say, $1$ foot long, you don't contract $10$ inches. Express your answer in terms of the side lengths of the rectangle.



My first instinct was to make a diagram, but since I was in the car at the time and don't have any paper, I couldn't. Is there an easy way to do this?



(I'm not sure if this should go in HSM/CSM, I posted it here because I thought it was more MSM level.)
